sentences.text: The name Invictibellatrix translates as “unconquered woman warrior” in Latin and is known from a single braincase from the Early Cretaceous Barremian Wessex Formation of England.
It is estimated to have weighed between 200 and 300 kilograms and measured about 4 meters in length.

Its skull shows three distinctive features: a small recessus basipterygoideus on each side of the parabasisphenoíd, a lightly transversely compressed hourglass-shaped crest, and curved depressions along the crest midline.
The holotype braincase (NHMUK PV R 6775) was recovered on the Isle of Wight and entered the Natural History Museum in London in May 1924.
Invictibellatrix was formally described as a new genus and species in 2026 by Cassius Morrison and colleagues.
To date, the only fossil material attributed to this taxon is that single braincase from the Wessex Formation.
Neurocranial characters such as a sub-circular occipital condyle, sub-oval foramen magnum, and a sagittal nuchal crest support its assignment to Megaraptora.
Phylogenetic analyses generally recover Invictibellatrix as a derived member of Megaraptoridae, a clade otherwise known mainly from Late Cretaceous Gondwana.
It lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.
The lack of megaraptorans in Late Cretaceous Laurasia is interpreted by some researchers as a regional extinction rather than a true absence.
